checks.claim: Wegener was a German meteorologist (weather scientist) and polar explorer; by 1912 he had already been on the 1906-08 Danmark expedition to Greenland
He first set out the idea in a lecture on 6 January 1912 to the Geologische Vereinigung (Geological Association) at the Senckenberg Museum in Frankfurt
checks.note: Wikipedia and the Environment & Society Portal give the same date and venue.

checks.claim: He later set it out in a book (Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane, 1915)
Key: the continents were once one land that broke up and drifted apart
checks.note: The 1915 book's single Urkontinent; the stem's 'later set out in a book' covers it.

checks.claim: Wrong: continents have stood in the same places since Earth was young (the permanence view, not his)
Wrong: continents rise and sink in place but never move sideways (the fixist view, not his)
Wrong: large parts of them sank to form the ocean floors (Suess-style sunken continents, which Wegener rejected on isostasy)
Context: most geologists of his day held that continents and oceans kept their places, rising or sinking at most; many saw him as an outsider
checks.note: Wikipedia notes wide European acceptance of the main tenets in the 1920s, but the context speaks of 1912, so it stands.

checks.claim: In December 1910 he wrote to his future wife asking whether the east coast of South America does not fit exactly against the west coast of Africa, as if once joined
About a year later (6 December 1911) he wrote to her father, Wladimir Koppen, that he came to the idea through the correspondence of the coastlines
checks.note: Scientific American gives 'I came to the idea on the grounds of the matching coastlines'. 'His whole idea had grown from it' is a fair paraphrase.

checks.claim: Key: the fit of two coasts across an ocean
Wrong: the same fossil reptile on two continents (he met the fossil papers only in autumn 1911, after the 1910 letter)
Wrong: matching rocks in mountains; coal under ice (later lines of evidence, not what he wrote of in 1910)
Context: others had seen the fit before him (Ortelius, Snider-Pellegrini)
Context: he saw the outlines match better along the continental shelves
checks.note: Wikipedia: from at least 1910 he imagined them fitting at the level of the continental shelves, about 200 m below the shore.

checks.claim: The 1915 book called the supercontinent the Urkontinent ('primal continent')
In the 1920 edition he used the name Pangaea 'instead', and that name stuck
checks.note: Wikipedia (and Krause, AWI) say he used 'Pangaea' only ONCE in the 1920 edition ('the Pangaea of the Carboniferous'), not in place of Urkontinent; the historian Celal Sengor dates the name to the 1922 third edition. So both 'instead' and the 1920 date are shaky. Fix: 'In a later edition he also used a name made of two Greek words, and that is the name that stuck: Pangaea.'

checks.claim: Key: Pangaea means 'all the land' (pan, all + Gaia/ge, earth or land)
checks.note: Britannica and Sengor gloss it 'all lands'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'the first land' (that is the sense of Ur-kontinent, not Pangaea), 'the great land', 'the lost land'
Context: one great ocean surrounded it (Panthalassa); it began to break apart about 200 million years ago
checks.note: Grokipedia: breakup began about 201 million years ago, at the end of the Triassic.

checks.claim: His two forces: a pole-fleeing push from Earth's spin (Polflucht) and tidal forces
checks.note: UCMP: 'centrifugal and tidal forces'.

checks.claim: Harold Jeffreys, a British geophysicist, calculated the forces
Key: the forces were far too weak to move a continent
checks.note: Sci Am: Jeffreys showed the forces 'much too weak or if strong enough, had to stop earth's rotation'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: just strong enough; faster than he said; strong enough to shatter a continent
Context: Jeffreys showed a tide strong enough to shift a continent would stop Earth turning in less than a year
checks.note: Holmes (1929/31), citing Jeffreys and Lambert: the force would have to be ten thousand million times stronger and 'would stop the earth's rotation altogether in about a year'. UCMP gives 'less than one year'. Close enough.

checks.claim: Context: 'Wegener could name no better force'
checks.note: In his 1929 fourth edition Wegener did name mantle convection currents as a possible cause (EGU 2015 abstract; found via search, not opened). He could not show any force was strong enough, which is the fair point. Fix: 'and Wegener could show no force strong enough'.

checks.claim: Quote: in 1929 he wrote 'the Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared'
checks.note: NASA quotes it from his last (1929) revision.

checks.claim: Mesosaurus was a small aquatic reptile; its fossils lie in Early Permian rocks of the same age in southern Africa (South Africa, Namibia) and South America (Brazil, Uruguay)
Key: the critics' usual answer was a land bridge that later sank
checks.note: UCMP: orthodox science explained the matching organisms by land bridges, now sunken. NASA speaks of a continent-sized bridge; 'a strip of land' is a fair simplification (the American 'isthmian links' were narrow).

checks.claim: Wrong: the reptiles swam across the ocean (it could not cross the open South Atlantic)
Wrong: floating logs; the same reptile arose on each land by itself (not the critics' explanation)
Context: Wegener answered that a bridge of light continental rock could not sink into denser sea-floor rock and vanish (isostasy)
checks.note: Sci Am quotes his letter: isostasy 'would oppose the sinking of a continent because it is lighter'.

checks.claim: Context: plate tectonics later did away with the need for the bridges
Tharp was kept off research ships as a woman and drew maps from ships' echo-sounding depths
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'women were barred from working on ships at the time'; Grokipedia: barred until 1968.

checks.claim: In 1952 she found a V-shaped valley running down the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
checks.note: Grokipedia: late 1952; Tharp's own account: six profiles, work begun in 1952.

checks.claim: Quote: Heezen said it looked too much like continental drift and dismissed it as "girl talk"
checks.note: Documented in Tharp's own 1999 chapter 'Connect the Dots' (reprinted by Columbia's State of the Planet): he groaned and said 'It cannot be. It looks too much like continental drift', and 'initially dismissed my interpretation of the profiles as "girl talk"'. The stem paraphrases the first remark and quotes only 'girl talk', which matches.

checks.claim: Key: undersea earthquakes lined up along the valley
checks.note: Tharp: superimposed on a light table, the epicentres 'lined up within the valley'.

checks.claim: Wrong: a submarine dive (Project FAMOUS, 1970s), satellite photos, the lab head taking her side (Ewing was a skeptic)
Context: Howard Foster plotted undersea earthquake epicentres for a cable-laying project; the overlay showed an active rift
checks.note: Tharp: Heezen hired Foster; Bell Laboratories was interested in laying new cables. (Wikipedia names a turbidity-current project; both fit.)

checks.claim: Context: Heezen came round in 1953; their later maps showed a ridge running round the globe
checks.note: Mid-1953 (Tharp; Grokipedia).

checks.claim: After WWII, magnetometers (first used to hunt submarines) were towed behind research ships over the sea floor
The sea floor is striped, bands running parallel to the ridges
Key: the stripes record flips (reversals) of Earth's magnetic field
checks.note: 'the stripes record reversals of Earth's magnetic field, not changes in its intensity' (USGS, quoted there).

checks.claim: Wrong: field weakening; more iron in seawater; a more active Sun
checks.note: The field does weaken during a reversal, but the stripes record the direction, so the weakened choice is not defensible as the answer.

checks.claim: Context: magnetite grains line up with the field as the lava cools and lock its direction in; a flip makes a compass point south
checks.note: Locked in below the Curie temperature.

checks.claim: Context: the magnetometer reads the bands as stronger and weaker, but they record direction
Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews, British scientists at Cambridge, published in 1963 (Nature, 7 September)
Their hypothesis implied a telling pattern of stripes
checks.note: The 1963 paper had blocks drifting away from the ridge centre, parallel to its crest; Wikipedia says Vine (and Morley) realized this means symmetric patterns. The 1963 profiles themselves did not show the symmetry clearly; it was shown later. The stem asks what the hypothesis predicts, which is sound.

checks.claim: Key: matching stripes on each side, in mirror image
Wrong: differing sides; stripes crossing the ridge; evenly spaced, equal widths (reversals are irregular)
A ship's readings two years later (Eltanin-19, measured 1965) showed it almost perfectly
checks.note: Measured 1965, presented 1966 by Pitman and Heirtzler; the west-to-east pattern 'nearly matches' the east-to-west.

checks.claim: Context: the 'magic profile', Eltanin, Pacific-Antarctic Ridge (far south Pacific), won over doubters; a two-headed tape recorder
checks.note: Wikipedia gives the 'twin-headed tape recorder' image.

checks.claim: Plate tectonics was accepted in the 1960s and grew out of drift
Key: he was wrong that the continents plough through the sea floor
checks.note: UCMP: 'Wegener's theory was wrong in one major point: continents do not plow through the ocean floor'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices are things he got right: once joined; same fossils on lands far apart; still moving today
checks.note: He believed they were still moving (his speed, 250 cm a year, was too high, but the movement is real).

checks.claim: Context: he pictured continents moving through the ocean floor like ice floes; critics said the sea floor was too firm, and they were right
checks.note: Kossmat (1926): oceanic crust too firm for continents to 'simply plough through'; Jeffreys: a rigid mantle.

checks.claim: Context: 'Harry Hess proposed in the early 1960s that the sea floor itself spreads out from the mid-ocean ridges, so the continents ride along on moving plates, sea floor and all'
checks.note: Hess did propose sea-floor spreading (1960, published 1962), with the continents carried along. But plates were not his idea: Linda Hall Library says 'the idea that the Earth's surface consists of discrete and separate plates was a concept not yet formulated in 1960'. Plates came later in the 1960s (Wilson, McKenzie, Morgan). As written the sentence gives Hess the plates. Fix: 'Harry Hess proposed in the early 1960s that the sea floor itself spreads out from the mid-ocean ridges, carrying the continents along. Later in the 1960s this grew into plate tectonics: whole plates, continents and sea floor together, move.'

checks.claim: Wegener died on the Greenland ice in 1930
checks.note: He left Eismitte on 1 November 1930 and died on the way; his body was found on 12 May 1931.

checks.claim: Harold Jeffreys lived until 1989 and never accepted drift
checks.note: Died 18 March 1989 at 97, 'without ever endorsing the theory'.

checks.claim: By the end of the 1960s almost all geologists agreed the continents move
checks.note: UCMP: 'By the late 1960s, plate tectonics was well supported and accepted by almost all geologists'. (A few Soviet holdouts do not spoil 'almost all'.)

checks.claim: Key: new evidence from the sea floor
checks.note: Mapped ocean ridges, earthquake belts and the magnetic data.

checks.claim: Wrong: an expanding Earth; proof of Wegener's forces (they were shown too weak); a vote
checks.note: The expanding Earth was a rival idea (Heezen held it for a time) and was never accepted.

checks.claim: Context: ridges and their rift, earthquakes along them, mirror-image stripes; Jeffreys right that the forces were too weak

unit_notes: Checked on the web 2026-11-26 (Grokipedia first, then Wikipedia, NASA, UCMP, Science News, Columbia's State of the Planet for Tharp's own account, Linda Hall Library, Holmes 1931 for the one-year figure). The Tharp quotes are documented in her own 1999 chapter 'Connect the Dots'. Fact sheet F5 should note that Sengor dates 'Pangaea' to the 1922 edition and that the 1920 use was only once. F24 should not give Hess the word 'plates'. F13/F16: Wegener's 1929 edition mentioned mantle convection as a possible cause, so 'no better force' is too strong. Britannica, Maricopa and CUNY pages refused the fetch (403).
